course.title: Hiring Decisions: Criteria Before Candidates
course.subtitle: How to run a fair selection now: set job-related criteria first, reach people widely, score everyone the same way, and keep a truthful record, in a climate that is changing.
course.scope: This is general information as of October 2026, not legal advice. This course is voluntary and does not count as the training Minn. Stat. 43A.21 requires; the state's own training does that.
course.treatment: 5 lessons, each with explanation, a practice situation, a knowledge check and a plan to try, plus a one-page job aid.
course.duration: About 65 minutes across five lessons. Take them in short sittings.
course.author: One DHS / One DSD — People, Access and Culture
course.coverAlt: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

objectives: Describe the pending federal suit and the legal climate accurately, including what has not changed.
Write job-related criteria and scoring anchors before you see any candidate.
Reach a wider pool without limiting who may apply.
Run a structured interview that is accessible and scored independently.
Make and record a decision on the criteria, and respond to pressure from any direction.
evidence: Compare the responses to the practice situation in each lesson.
Answer the knowledge check in each lesson.
Use the job aid with a decision you choose.
learning.appliedNextStep: Before you next fill a position, sit down with Human Resources with the position description. Ask what order the contract and DHS procedure require, what tools they already provide, and how hiring justification works today. Then write your criteria and scoring anchors before any application reaches you.

lessons.title: The climate, and what holds steady
lessons.summary: Hiring is one of the most contested parts of equity work right now, and DHS is directly involved. This lesson says what is known, what is not, and what stays steady for a supervisor filling a job this month.

blocks.heading: Why hiring is an equity decision
blocks.body:
Hiring decides who gets access to public jobs, and those are good jobs. Research suggests that how you hire can change who gets through. In a review of 31 studies, Black and Hispanic applicants were rated about a quarter of a standard deviation lower on average in interviews, and high-structure interviews showed smaller group differences. In one retail firm, non-Black managers hired more white and fewer Black workers than Black managers did. Discrimination and unnecessary barriers in hiring are real concerns, and disabled applicants face barriers of their own.

So this course is direct about equity. The tools it teaches apply to everyone, and that is part of why they hold up.

blocks.heading: The pending suit, as of October 2026

tabs.label: What it is
tabs.body: United States v. Minnesota, No. 0:26-cv-00273 (D. Minn.). The U.S. Department of Justice filed on January 14, 2026, challenging Minnesota's affirmative action system under Title VII. A docket summary also lists Title VI.

tabs.label: What it targets
tabs.body: Law firm and docket summaries report that the suit cites provisions including Minn. Stat. 43A.19, 43A.191, subd. 3(c), and related rules. Section 43A.191, subd. 3(c) says an agency missing its hiring goals "must justify its nonaffirmative action hires." The docket summary lists DHS's Hiring Justification Policy as an exhibit. This course's authors did not read that exhibit or the amended complaint.

tabs.label: Where it stands
tabs.body: As reported by the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse (viewed October 31, 2026): an amended complaint was filed on September 11, 2026; fact discovery runs to March 1, 2027; dispositive motions are due by July 15, 2027; and no relief has been granted. One news report says the amendment narrows the case to a facial challenge with forward-looking relief. A preservation order was also reported in September 2026.

tabs.label: What each side says
tabs.body: DOJ is reported to be asking courts to overrule Weber and Johnson, older Supreme Court decisions that have allowed some employer affirmative action plans. In 2025, when DOJ opened its investigation, DHS was reported as saying the requirement rests on state law. A ruling could come while you are in this job. Check for updates.

tabs.label: What it does not mean
tabs.body: It does not mean the state has been found to have broken the law. It does not mean you may discriminate in any direction. It does not mean you should stop reaching out widely or removing barriers. It also does not mean the statutes have been struck down.

items.title: One standard for all employees
items.body: Ames (2025) held that majority-group employees do not face a higher bar under Title VII. The plaintiff worked at a state agency, and the acts challenged were a denied promotion and a demotion.

items.title: EEOC and DOJ positions
items.body: The EEOC's March 2025 technical assistance says there is no "diversity interest" exception and that client preference is no defense to race or color discrimination. These are agency positions, not law, and the document has not been refreshed since Ames. DOJ's July 2025 guidance is described as non-binding, though OMB directs federal agencies to follow it.

items.title: Disparate impact
items.body: Federal agencies have largely stepped back from it. HHS removed its Title VI disparate impact provisions effective July 24, 2026. An opinion from DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel, reported in June 2026, says the EEOC's Title VII framework is unconstitutional; it binds federal agencies and not courts. But Title VII's own disparate impact provision still exists, and private suits remain possible. The Minnesota Human Rights Act separately prohibits "a system of employment which unreasonably excludes" applicants (Minn. Stat. 363A.08, subd. 2). So do not teach or assume that disparate impact is dead, or that it is enforced as before.

items.title: Selection guidelines
items.body: The EEOC is reported to have sent a final rule rescinding its part of the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures to federal reviewers on October 16, 2026. The text was not public when this course was written. Do not treat that as permission to use a selection test with no job connection. State law and job-relatedness remain good reasons to tie every screen to the work.

items.title: Disability
items.body: Disability duties in hiring continue. Under HR/LR Policy 1433, agencies must provide reasonable accommodation so that a qualified applicant with a disability has an equal opportunity to compete, and notice of the policy goes on all job announcements. Minn. Stat. 43A.191, subd. 2a also addresses staff support for disability hiring.

blocks.body: Decide on job-related criteria, set before you see candidates. Apply them the same way to everyone. Do not weigh race, sex, disability or any other protected trait in choosing an individual. Remove barriers and reach widely before the decision.

blocks.heading: How to read that rule
blocks.body:
That rule is what this course teaches for a supervisor's individual selection. It does not take a side in the lawsuit. If anyone tells you a rule requires or permits you to weigh a protected trait in a particular selection, ask Human Resources for the written basis. Other sections of state law can raise agency-level duties, such as justification, and those go through Human Resources. Lesson 5 covers them.

Write every note and email in hiring as though an applicant, a steward, a state reviewer and a federal attorney might read it. That is not a threat. It is a reason to write what is true.

blocks.heading: Steady in a noisy climate
blocks.control: You control whether news about the case changes your process without anyone telling you to.
blocks.failure: Do not drop your outreach or your accommodation notices because of a headline. Do not start making comments about "needing" a certain kind of candidate because of a plan or a goal.
blocks.next: When you hear something new about the law, ask Human Resources: "Does this change what I do on this hire?" Until they say yes, keep the same process.

blocks.question: Which statement about disparate impact is accurate as of October 2026?

options.text: It has been abolished everywhere.
It is enforced by federal agencies as it always was.
Federal agencies have largely stepped back, but Title VII's provision still exists, and Minnesota law has its own text.
It applies only to private employers.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The practical answer is to tie every screen to the work.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Neither "dead" nor "as before" is accurate. Federal enforcement has moved. The statutes remain, including Minn. Stat. 363A.08's "unreasonably excludes" text.

learning.objective: Describe United States v. Minnesota as reported in October 2026.
objectives: Describe United States v. Minnesota as reported in October 2026.
Separate federal enforcement positions from statutes and court rulings.
Explain why disparate impact is neither dead nor enforced as before.
State the working rule for individual selections in this course.
takeaways: The suit is pending. Reported as of October 2026, no court has granted relief.
The state's statutes remain on the books while they are challenged.
Your job is the same in any outcome: job-related criteria, applied the same way, with an honest record.

scenario.context: You are about to fill a waiver consultant position. In the hallway, one colleague tells you, "With that lawsuit, I'd take out the community outreach list and skip the panel. Just hire who you know." Another says, "The statute's still there. You should really make sure this hire helps our numbers."

options.label: Follow the first colleague. The safest step in a lawsuit is to do as little as possible.
options.response: Hiring who you know is the least defensible choice here. It has no stated criteria and no record, and it keeps the pool narrow. Nothing in the reported status of the suit requires you to drop outreach or panels.

options.label: Follow the second colleague, and keep the numbers in mind when you choose.
options.response: Weighing a protected trait in an individual selection is what this course teaches you not to do. Agency-level goals and justification go through Human Resources. They do not mean you, on your own, should favor a candidate because of a trait.

options.label: Thank them both and call Human Resources. Ask what process applies now, including any justification step. Set job-related criteria first, keep open outreach, use structured interviews and record your reasons.
options.response: This holds up whichever way the case goes. It keeps the pool wide and the decision job-related, and it sends agency-level questions to the people who handle them.

options.label: Hold off on the hire until the case is decided.
options.response: Dispositive motions alone are reported as running to mid-2027. The work and the people served cannot wait. There is also no reason to think a fair process needs to wait.

transfer.prompt: Think of your next hire or one you might join as a panelist. "If someone tells me the lawsuit means I should change my process, then I will ask [Human Resources contact] what, if anything, has changed, and until then I will keep [criteria first, open outreach, structured scoring, honest records]."
options: Ask Human Resources how hiring justification works today in your division.
Ask whom to check with when the court rules.
Save this course's date. Legal facts here are as of October 2026.

lessons.title: Criteria before candidates
lessons.summary: Once you have seen a résumé, you will start to bend your criteria to fit the person you like. This lesson teaches you to set criteria and anchors first, using behavior in place of vague traits.

blocks.heading: Build the criteria
items: Read the position description and class specification. Ask Human Resources for both.
List the essential duties. Talk with someone who does this job now.
For each duty, name what a person must be able to do on day one, and what you can teach.
Choose four to six criteria that matter most.
Decide how you will measure each: a question, a work sample, a reference.
Write what weak, solid and strong look like for each one.
Date the document. Give it to Human Resources. Do not change it after applications come in without talking to them.

tabs.label: "Five years at a lead agency"
tabs.body: Ask what skill you actually want. Perhaps it is knowing how waiver case management works. Someone might have learned this at a county, a Tribal agency, a provider or as a family caregiver navigating the system. Describe the skill, and let more routes count. Check with Human Resources how this fits the class specification.

tabs.label: "Valid driver's license"
tabs.body: If the job involves site visits, the need is getting to sites. A license may exclude some disabled applicants who could use other transportation. If driving is not essential, say "able to travel to sites." Ask the ADA coordinator if unsure.

tabs.label: "Bachelor's degree preferred"
tabs.body: If the degree stands in for writing or analysis, test writing and analysis. Minnesota law prohibits a system of employment that "unreasonably excludes" applicants, and a work sample shows you more about the skill anyway.

tabs.label: "Excellent verbal communication"
tabs.body: Does the job require speaking, or does it require communicating? An applicant who is Deaf and uses an interpreter may communicate excellently. An applicant who has an accent may be very clear. Write what the communication has to accomplish.

tabs.label: "Strong culture fit"
tabs.body: Take this one out. It is too easy for this to mean "someone like us." Replace it with the behaviors you actually need, such as "raises concerns early," or "takes direction and gives feedback respectfully."

blocks.heading: Making cultural competence a skill
blocks.body:
Minn. Stat. 43A.21 uses the term "cultural competence" for supervisor training, and the National Frontline Supervisor Competencies include culturally competent selection. It is a real skill in DSD's work, where staff work with people using interpreters, families from many communities, and people with many kinds of disabilities.

To make it fair and job-related, state it as behavior, applicable to any applicant, with no assumption from their background:

  • "Explains a waiver change so that a family using an interpreter can make a real choice."
  • "Checks understanding, and does not assume it."
  • "Adjusts materials for literacy level and format."
  • "Asks what the person wants, and follows person-centered plans."
  • "Responds when a coworker or provider says something demeaning."

Washington State publishes sample hiring questions built on behaviors like these. You can write your own for the actual job.

Do not assume someone has this skill because of who they are. Do not assume they lack it, either. Ask everyone the same question, and score the answer.

items.title: Language skills
items.body: If the job needs Hmong, Somali, Spanish, ASL or another language, state it as a skill and a level, and check it for every applicant the same way. Do not infer it from a name or background. Ask Human Resources how to post and verify it, and whether it affects classification or pay. The EEOC's statement on customer preference is about race and color. A stated, tested language skill is different from choosing someone because of who you assume families would prefer. Ask Human Resources if a proposal drifts toward the latter.

items.title: Tests and inventories
items.body: Do not use results from this app, Cultural Intelligence assessments or the Intercultural Development Inventory (IDI) in a selection. This app promises that no such results go into selection criteria, and the IDI's validity for BIPOC respondents is disputed in published work.

items.title: Hiring supervisors and managers
items.body: DHS's Affirmative Action Plan for July 2024 to June 2026 said DHS would assess managers and supervisors at hire for "cultural competency, authenticity, courage, and will." That plan's period has ended, and this course's authors did not find a 2026-2028 plan. Ask Human Resources what applies now. Whatever the plan says, words like "authenticity" and "courage" need to be turned into behaviors tied to the job before they can be scored fairly. For example: "Gave a hard message to a leader, and describe what happened."

items.title: People who use services on panels
items.body: The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies include hiring with participants and families. If you want people who use services to take part, ask Human Resources how to do that, and give them the same criteria and sheet as everyone else. Plan for their access needs, and do not ask them to represent a whole community.

blocks.heading: Date it first
blocks.control: You control whether the criteria exist before you know the people.
blocks.failure: Do not write the criteria around someone you already have in mind. Do not rewrite them after you have seen who applied.
blocks.next: Save a dated copy of the criteria with Human Resources before the posting closes. If you need to make changes, talk to Human Resources, and record why.

blocks.question: Which is the best way to include cultural competence in criteria?

options.text: Prefer candidates from the communities the program serves.
Rate how comfortable the panel feels with the candidate.
Use the IDI score from an assessment.
Ask every candidate how they have explained a service change to a family using an interpreter, and score it with anchors.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Yes. It makes the skill observable and job-related, and it is the same for everyone.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Look again. Don't assume the skill from identity, comfort or an inventory. Ask about behavior and score it the same way for everyone.

learning.objective: Derive criteria from the job's actual duties.
objectives: Derive criteria from the job's actual duties.
Separate what is required on day one from what can be learned.
Test each requirement for unnecessary barriers.
Write equity-related skills as observable behaviors.
State a language requirement as a skill.
takeaways: Write it down before you see anyone.
Every requirement should tie to a duty.
Cultural competence is something a person does, so ask about what they did.

scenario.context: You are drafting criteria for a program consultant who will support waiver providers. A temporary employee has been doing similar work, and you think highly of them. Your draft says: "Three years of experience in this unit's waiver program; strong verbal presence; valid driver's license; good culture fit." The job includes some travel, a lot of written guidance and frequent phone and video calls with providers.

options.label: Keep the draft. These are real things you want, and you know that the temporary employee would do the job well.
options.response: The draft closely fits one person. "This unit's" experience may shut out strong applicants with the same skills, and "presence" and "fit" are hard to score fairly. It would be hard to explain in a review.

options.label: Rewrite it from the duties: knowledge of waiver rules, writing clear guidance, explaining things to providers, getting to sites. Ask the ADA coordinator or Human Resources about the license, and write anchors for each. Use the same process for the temporary employee as for anyone else.
options.response: This is the strongest move. The temporary employee can still shine on job-related criteria, and now other people can as well. Check the order required by the contract and by HR before planning the rest of the process.

options.label: Remove all criteria that the temporary employee would pass easily, so that the process is more open.
options.response: This overcorrects by building the criteria against someone. The swap test applies here too. Let the job's duties set the criteria.

transfer.prompt: Consider the next role you may fill. "If I am writing criteria for [role], then I will start from [the duties], test each requirement by asking [who it would exclude and why it matters], and date the criteria before I see any applicants."
options: Get the position description and class specification.
Talk to someone who does the job now.
Choose which vague words to replace.

lessons.title: Reach widely, and keep the door open
lessons.summary: A fair decision among a narrow pool is still a narrow decision. This lesson covers contract order, open outreach and what research says about recruitment messages.

blocks.heading: Who comes first
blocks.body:
If the vacancy is in a MAPE position, Article 16 of the 2025-2027 contract sets an order you must follow, and Human Resources will walk you through it. In short:

  • The vacancy is posted for a minimum of seven calendar days, with the division, section, classification, employment condition, minimum qualifications and location.
  • Eligible employees in the seniority unit may interest bid. Qualified bidders get consideration and may be appointed before other applicants. Seniority of bidders is not a factor in choosing among them. The employer "shall not be arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory and must have a legitimate business reason to reject all of the interest bidders." Bidders are told their status in a timely way.
  • Next come the seniority unit layoff list and claims from employees facing layoff.
  • Then come other means, including a multi-source recruitment and selection process.

So your plan to do wide outreach or to use a certain interview may only come into play later. Other agreements have their own rules, so check them. Do not promise anyone a process before you know which one applies.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: In a randomized study of police recruiting, postcards with challenge or career messages were three times as effective as a control, and particularly effective for people of color and women, while public-service messages were not effective. In a randomized study at a financial firm, explicit diversity signaling in recruiting materials more than doubled minority interest, applications and selection. Both are specific settings. Neither shows what will happen at DHS.

tabs.label: Where to go
tabs.body: Share the posting through community organizations, disability organizations, cultural media, professional groups, colleges, and networks of direct support and interpreting professionals across Minnesota, including greater Minnesota. Ask Human Resources which channels they use and what is allowed.

tabs.label: What to say
tabs.body: Describe the work, the challenge and the career path. Say who the work serves. You can say that the agency wants a wide range of people to apply. Ask Human Resources to look over any statement about diversity, given the EEOC's current position.

tabs.label: What to avoid
tabs.body: Do not write or imply that the job is for people of a certain background. Do not hold special information sessions open only to some groups. The EEOC says limiting access and separating people by protected characteristic can be unlawful. Keep every event open to anyone.

tabs.label: Access
tabs.body: Under Policy 1433, notice of the policy belongs on all job announcements. An applicant may ask any agency official they have contact with during the process for an accommodation, and the request needs no special words. Forward it promptly. Check that the application works with assistive technology. Give a contact who can respond. Offer captioned or interpreted information sessions.

blocks.heading: The informal shoulder tap
blocks.body:
You may know someone who would be great. You can tell them about the posting. So far, so good, but offer the same help to everyone. Do not review their résumé, tell them the questions or give them hints you do not give to others. If you know them well, tell Human Resources, and ask if you should step off the panel.

The same goes for temporary and acting staff. They have an advantage in knowing the work. That may be real knowledge, and it can show up in scores. Do not add to it by sharing inside information.

blocks.heading: Same information for all
blocks.control: You control what any applicant learns from you outside the process.
blocks.failure: Do not answer a candidate's question privately if the answer would help them, unless you are willing to give it to everyone.
blocks.next: Keep a short list of what you will say about the job, and use it for every inquiry. Route process questions to Human Resources.

blocks.question: Under the MAPE contract, which is true of interest bidders?

options.text: The most senior bidder must be appointed.
Seniority of bidders is not a factor in appointing among them. Bidders who qualify get consideration first.
Interest bids are considered only after an open search.
A supervisor can reject all bidders with no reason.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct, under Article 16, Section 4. Rejecting all bidders requires a legitimate business reason, and the process may not be arbitrary, capricious or discriminatory.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Check Article 16, Section 4. Qualified bidders are considered first, seniority is not a factor among them, and rejecting all bidders needs a legitimate business reason.

learning.objective: Describe the MAPE contract's order for filling a vacancy.
objectives: Describe the MAPE contract's order for filling a vacancy.
Plan open outreach that widens the pool without limiting who may apply.
Make the application process accessible.
Treat internal candidates and informal contacts fairly.
takeaways: Check the order first. You may not be free to start with an open search.
Tell more people. Do not narrow who may apply.

scenario.context: You will fill a position through a multi-source process, after Human Resources confirms no interest bidders or layoff list applies. You want to reach more applicants, including people with waiver experience in the Somali and Hmong communities and disabled people with direct experience of services. A colleague suggests you phone a few community leaders and ask them to send "their best people" to you directly, and you would then put these people through to an early conversation.

options.label: Follow the suggestion. Your purpose is good, and you need to reach these communities.
options.response: Your purpose is good, but an early conversation for some candidates gives them an advantage, and it is tied to who referred them and which community they come from. It may look like what the EEOC warns against. Keep the outreach, and lose the side door.

options.label: Skip outreach altogether. In this climate, you should just post it and wait.
options.response: Nothing in the reported status of the suit requires you to do this. Posting and waiting keeps the pool as narrow as your current networks. Wider outreach open to anyone is a low-cost step with some randomized evidence behind it, in other settings.

options.label: Share the posting widely, including with those community and disability organizations and with other networks. Offer an open information session anyone can attend, with access arranged. Send every applicant through the same process.
options.response: This is the strongest move. It widens who hears about the job and keeps the same door for everyone. Ask Human Resources about the wording.

options.label: Ask Human Resources to add a preference for candidates from those communities to the posting.
options.response: That builds a protected trait into the selection. If you want to reach people with specific skills, such as language or lived experience of navigating services, state the skill or experience itself, in terms anyone could meet. Talk to Human Resources about how.

transfer.prompt: Plan your next outreach. "If I am filling [role], then I will first confirm [the required order] with Human Resources, share the posting through [three networks you do not usually reach], and treat every inquiry the same."
options: Who has never heard of this kind of job at DHS?
Is the application accessible? Have you tried it with a screen reader?
Who will respond to accommodation requests from applicants?

lessons.title: Same questions, same scoring
lessons.summary: Structured interviews are among the best-supported tools you have. This lesson shows how to run one, how to make it accessible, and what to do when a panelist goes off-script.

blocks.heading: What the evidence supports, and its limits
blocks.body:
A 2022 re-analysis ranked structured interviews as the top selection procedure after correcting for overestimated validities. That paper has drawn significant criticism, so hold the ranking loosely. An earlier review found smaller group differences with high-structure interviews. In one organization, with nearly 20,000 applicants for a managerial-level job, neither applicant race or gender nor interviewer similarity affected ratings in highly structured interviews. That was observational, and it concerns one employer.

Formalization is not magic. Written job tests for managers were followed by declines for several groups in one long-running corporate study. Removing names from applications has mixed results: Australian public servants shortlisted identified minority candidates more often than de-identified ones, and French firms that opted into anonymous résumés became less likely to interview and hire minority candidates. So do not assume any single tool settles the matter. Also, no study here measured DSD's own hiring. Ask Human Resources what your unit already uses. If what it provides differs from this lesson, start with theirs, and discuss any gaps.

blocks.heading: Building the interview
items: Write four to six questions tied to your criteria. Ask about past behavior ("Tell me about a time...") or a realistic work problem.
Ask every candidate the same questions, in the same order. Follow-ups should be neutral, such as "What happened next?"
Write anchors for each question: what weak, solid and strong answers include.
Add a work sample if the job needs one, such as writing guidance on a waiver change.
Send the questions in advance, if your practice permits. It can help everyone, including people who process language differently or use interpreters. Do it for all candidates or none.

Keep a sheet with only these questions. Nothing about health, family, faith, national origin, age or plans for children belongs on it. If a candidate brings any of that up, do not write it down or follow up on it.

blocks.heading: A sample question with anchors
blocks.body:
Question: "Tell me about a time you had to explain a change in a program or service to someone who was upset or who was using an interpreter. What did you do to check they understood?"

Weak: Describes telling the person the rule. No check for understanding. Blames the person or the interpreter.

Solid: Gives a real example. Speaks to the person and not the interpreter. Checks understanding. Follows up.

Strong: All of the above, and adjusts format or timing, involves the person in what happens next, and learns something that changes their practice.

items.title: Who sits on it
items.body: Include people who know the work. Train panelists first. Multnomah County has offered interview panel training and tracked panel representation. A range of perspectives on a panel can help, and asking the same person to serve on every panel because of who they are is another matter. That is extra work assigned by identity, so count it and offer it broadly. Ask Human Resources about any panel rules.

items.title: Score alone first
items.body: Each panelist scores each answer against the anchors, right after the candidate leaves, before anyone speaks. Then talk. Speaking first tends to steer the room.

items.title: Accessible interviews
items.body: Ask all candidates in the same way whether they need anything to take part. Forward requests promptly, and consult the ADA coordinator on questions. Book qualified interpreters or CART when asked. Interview format, timing and technology may all need to change. Look at the candidate when you speak, even if an interpreter is present. Do not lower your standards, and do not score slower pacing that comes from interpretation.

items.title: Equal time
items.body: Keep to similar times. A long, warm chat with one person and a brisk session with another is a difference in treatment, even when the questions match.

items.title: Conflict of interest
items.body: If a panelist knows a candidate well, tell Human Resources before scoring.

blocks.heading: What to say when a panelist goes off-script

tabs.label: "Not a good fit"
tabs.body: "Which criterion is that? What did they say that fell short of the anchor?"

tabs.label: "That accent will be hard for families"
tabs.body: "Our criterion is whether they explain things clearly. How did they score on that question?" A comment like this may raise national origin issues. Tell Human Resources if it persists, or if someone says it about a candidate's identity.

tabs.label: "Too polished for our families"
tabs.body: "That's an assumption about the families. What in the answer does or does not show the skill?"

tabs.label: "She'd be great, she reminds me of me"
tabs.body: "What did she say that met the anchor?" Similarity can feel like evidence. You do not need to accuse anyone. Just go back to the sheet.

blocks.body: The sheet protects the candidate, and it also protects the panel. When you are unsure, go back to it.

blocks.heading: Back to the sheet
blocks.control: You control the discussion if you chair the panel.
blocks.failure: Do not let the first or most senior speaker set the score. Do not let a comment about someone's identity pass as a comment about their fitness.
blocks.next: Open each discussion with: "Let's go through scores first. Where do we differ, and what did the candidate actually say?"

blocks.question: When should panelists first share their views on a candidate?

options.text: During the interview, using the chat.
After each panelist has scored independently against the anchors.
Before the interview, based on the résumé.
After the chair states their view, for efficiency.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Scoring first keeps early or senior voices from steering the room.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Look again. Have each person score independently against the anchors, then discuss.

learning.objective: Build a structured interview: same questions, same order, scored anchors.
objectives: Build a structured interview: same questions, same order, scored anchors.
Score independently before any panel discussion.
Run an accessible interview.
Respond to comments on fit, accent or personal matters.
takeaways: Score the answer, not the delivery.

scenario.context: You chair a panel for a case consultant position. Two candidates scored about the same. After the second interview, a senior panelist says, "The first one felt right. The second one is really qualified, but she's got that accent, and I just wonder how families will take it. Also, the first one has kids, so I know they'd get what families go through." The other panelist looks uncomfortable. You have not yet collected the score sheets.

options.label: Let it go for now, and hope the scores sort it out. You do not want a scene.
options.response: Unaddressed, this will shape the discussion and possibly the outcome. It also leaves your other panelist alone. You can address it calmly, without a scene.

options.label: Tell the panelist that was discriminatory, and remove them from the panel on the spot.
options.response: You may need to raise this further, but you do not have that authority alone, and a confrontation can derail the process. Bring the group back to the criteria and talk to Human Resources.

options.label: Say, "Let's stick to the sheet. Accent and family status aren't on it. Our criterion is explaining things clearly, so what did each candidate say?" Collect independent scores before discussing further. Tell Human Resources what was said, and ask whether anything further is needed.
options.response: This is the strongest move. It stops the comment from entering the decision, models the behavior and gets the right people involved. Comments about accent can raise national origin issues, and family status has no place on the sheet.

transfer.prompt: Plan your next interview. "If a panelist says something that is not on the sheet, then I will say [my sentence] and go back to [the criterion]. If it touches on a protected trait, I will tell [Human Resources contact] the same day."
options: Write your sentence for "not a good fit."
Ask Human Resources what panel training is available.
Write anchors for one question this week.

lessons.title: Deciding, justifying, and keeping the record
lessons.summary: This lesson covers making the final choice, what to do with pressure from any direction, how justification fits in, and which records to keep.

blocks.heading: Comparing and choosing
blocks.body:
Lay out the finalists side by side, on each criterion. In a lab study, evaluating candidates jointly shifted decisions from stereotypes toward performance. Your scores are not a machine. You can use judgment, as long as you can tie it to the job and write it down. If the numbers point one way and you want to go another, explain why with reference to the criteria.

Under the MAPE contract, when a multi-source process is used, Article 16, Section 4(C)(1) says selection among finalists is based on "skill, ability, experience, efficiency, job knowledge and/or fitness to perform the duties of the position." If two or more finalists are equal on those factors and one or more is in the bargaining unit, a bargaining unit employee in a different class or option is selected. Other agreements differ, so check with Human Resources before you decide. Do not treat that tie rule as something you can apply casually.

Also check references the same way for each finalist, with the same questions, and only with what Human Resources allows.

tabs.label: "We need to hire more ___"
tabs.body: A leader or colleague says the team needs someone from a particular race, sex or community. The answer: "I'll go back to the criteria. If there's a rule that changes this, please point me to it, and I'll ask Human Resources." If you think the skill is what is really needed, such as a language, state it as a skill for the next hire.

tabs.label: "We've hired too many ___"
tabs.body: A leader or colleague says the team has too many people of a certain group, or that a choice will look like a quota. The answer is the same. It does not change because the group changed. Ames applies the same standard to everyone.

tabs.label: Orders
tabs.body: The EEOC lists refusing an instruction that would lead to discrimination as protected activity. If you are directed to weigh a trait, or you see it happening, go to Human Resources. Policy 1436 requires you to report possible discrimination immediately, to Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer.

tabs.label: Goals and plans
tabs.body: State law sets affirmative action goals at the agency level and requires agency plans. That law is under challenge, and it is on the books as of October 2026. Agency plans go through Human Resources and the commissioner. They do not give an individual supervisor a separate authority to favor anyone. Ask Human Resources how the plan touches your hire.

blocks.heading: If a justification is required
blocks.body:
Minn. Stat. 43A.191, subd. 3(c) says an agency missing its hiring goals "must justify its nonaffirmative action hires." DHS has a Hiring Justification Policy, which is reported to be an exhibit in the federal suit. This course's authors have not read it, and do not describe its steps. Ask Human Resources whether it applies to your hire and how it works today.

If you are asked to write one, here is the general rule. Write the truth, using your dated criteria and scores. Name the job-related reasons for your selection. Do not change who you pick so that you can avoid paperwork, and do not change the paperwork to fit a reason you did not actually use. Do not add comments about anyone's race, sex or disability that were not part of what you were asked to record. If you do not understand what you are being asked, ask.

blocks.heading: What to keep
items: The dated criteria and anchors.
The posting and where it was shared.
Each panelist's score sheet, with no later changes.
Your written reason for the selection.
Any accommodation steps, kept separately and confidentially according to Human Resources' direction.
Notes of any issues raised and what was done.

blocks.body: A preservation order is reported to have been entered in the federal suit in September 2026. The sources behind this course do not establish whether it reaches a unit's hiring files. So do not delete, tidy or rewrite anything from a hiring process without asking Human Resources how long to keep it and where to store it. Also ask how applicant data is classified under the Data Practices Act.

blocks.heading: After the hire
blocks.body:
Tell candidates through the process Human Resources sets. If you give feedback, base it on the criteria. Bidders under the MAPE contract are told their status in a timely way.

Then the hire becomes your onboarding job. Everyone needs the same introduction, a peer or mentor if your practice provides one, and early access needs met. Under Article 16, Section 6, wherever practicable a new employee on probation gets a performance counseling review at about the midpoint. Plan it now.

When the process is over, review it privately: Were criteria set first? Were scores independent? Did you reach beyond your usual networks? Did anyone drop out because of an access problem? Use the answers on the next hire. No check in this course can tell you whether your hire was fair, and a single hire shows very little about a pattern. Bring what you find to Human Resources if it points to a barrier in the process.

blocks.heading: One answer in both directions
blocks.control: You control whether your answer to pressure changes with the source or the direction.
blocks.failure: Do not agree in the hallway to avoid a conflict. Do not write down a reason you did not use.
blocks.next: Practice saying this: "I'm going by the criteria we set. If there's a rule that changes that, please show me, and I'll check with Human Resources."

blocks.question: What should you do with panel score sheets after you have made a hire?

options.text: Destroy them to protect candidates' privacy.
Rewrite them so that they match the final decision.
Keep them unchanged, and ask Human Resources how long and where to keep them.
Share them with the team so that they can see the process was fair.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A truthful record protects candidates, you and the agency. Do not delete or rewrite anything without asking.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Look again. Do not destroy, rewrite or share these. Keep them unchanged, and ask Human Resources about retention.

learning.objective: Make a selection by comparing candidates on the record.
objectives: Make a selection by comparing candidates on the record.
Respond to pressure to weigh a protected trait, in any direction.
Write a truthful justification if one is required.
Keep hiring records, and ask about preservation.
takeaways: The same answer holds, whichever direction the pressure comes from.
A justification states what happened. It never changes what happened.
Keep your records. Do not tidy up.

scenario.context:
Version A: Your panel's scores are close, with a white candidate slightly ahead. Your director says, "Look at this unit. Everyone is white. I need you to pick the other candidate, who is Black. You know why."

Version B: Your panel's scores are close, with a Black candidate slightly ahead. Your director says, "With this lawsuit, I don't want anything that looks like a diversity hire. Pick the other candidate, who is white. You know why."
scenario.prompt: What do you do next in each version?

options.label: Follow the direction in both. Your director outranks you, and the scores were close.
options.response: A close score does not change what the instruction is. It is an instruction to choose based on race. Following it could expose you, and it would harm a candidate in either version.

options.label: Follow Version A, because of the state's goals, and refuse Version B.
options.response: The swap test catches this. An individual supervisor being told to pick someone by race is the same problem in both versions. Agency goals do not hand you that decision, and Ames sets one standard for everyone.

options.label: In both versions, say you will decide on the criteria, and ask for any written basis. Compare the finalists on the record. Report the instruction to Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer right away, and write down what was said and when.
options.response: This is the strongest move. It gives one answer in both directions, keeps the decision tied to the job and puts the matter with the people who must handle it. The EEOC treats refusing an order that would lead to discrimination as protected activity.

options.label: Step off the hire, and let your director decide.
options.response: You might raise this with Human Resources, but stepping away on your own leaves the candidates exposed and the instruction unreported. Policy 1436 requires you to report.

transfer.prompt: Plan for pressure. "If anyone tells me to choose or avoid someone because of a protected trait, in either direction, then I will say [my sentence], report it to [Human Resources or Affirmative Action Officer contact] the same day, and keep my decision on the criteria."
options: Write your sentence, and say it aloud.
Ask Human Resources how the Hiring Justification Policy works today.
Ask where to keep hiring records, and for how long.

jobAid.title: Hiring: criteria before candidates
jobAid.subtitle: Legal facts as of October 2026. Check with Human Resources for changes, including any ruling in United States v. Minnesota.

use.purpose: To help you run a selection you can explain to anyone who asks.
remember: Decide on job-related criteria set before you see candidates.
Do not weigh race, sex, disability or any other protected trait in an individual selection.
Reach widely. Keep every door open to anyone.
Same answer to pressure in any direction.
Write what is true, and keep it.
use.doNext: Call Human Resources before your next vacancy opens, and ask what they already provide.

sections.heading: Before posting
items: Ask Human Resources about the required order: under MAPE Article 16, posting, interest bids, layoff lists, claims, then other means. Check other agreements.
Get the position description. Write four to six criteria from the duties, with anchors. Date them.
Test each requirement: who does it exclude, and does the job need it?
State language needs as skills. State cultural competence as behaviors.
Do not use cultural intelligence, IDI or results from this app.
Ask how justification works today.

sections.heading: Reaching people
items: Share widely, including disability and community networks and greater Minnesota.
Keep events and messages open to anyone.
Include the accommodation notice. Forward any request promptly.
Give the same information to everyone.

sections.heading: The interview
items: Same questions, same order, same time. Neutral follow-ups.
Nothing about health, family, faith, national origin or age.
Arrange access early. Score the answer, not the delivery.
Score independently first. Then discuss.
When someone says "fit": "Which criterion? What did they say?"

sections.heading: The decision
items: Compare side by side, and write a reason tied to the criteria.
If directed to weigh a trait: decide on criteria, ask for any written basis, and report to Human Resources or the Affirmative Action Officer.
If justification is required: write the truth, from your dated records.
Keep criteria, scores and reasons unchanged. Ask about retention and preservation.
